21                                      INTRODUCTION AND PARTIES

22        1. Plaintiff International Technological University Foundation (“ITU”) is a global

23              multiethnic nonprofit institution of higher education based in Santa Clara, California. ITU
24              was founded in 1994 by Professor Shu-Park Chan to be the world’s first global university
25
                network model. ITU emphasizes the STEM fields (Science, Technology, Engineering and
26
                Mathematics) in its course offerings. ITU’s student body has largely been comprised of
27
                international students, predominately from India and the People’s Republic of China.
28


     4907-7867-5263.12
           Case 5:25-cv-08277           Document 1        Filed 09/29/25      Page 2 of 12



 1              ITU’s commitment to protecting the rights of its international multiethnic students has
 2              resulted in it facing racial discrimination, including from Defendant in this matter.
 3
          2. Defendant WASC Senior College and University Commission (“WSCUC”) is a California
 4
                nonprofit corporation headquartered in Alameda, California. WSCUC was originally part
 5
                of the Western Association of Schools and Colleges (“WASC”), which was formed on
 6

 7              March 12, 1962. WSCUC split off from WASC and filed separate Articles of

 8              Incorporation on December 21, 2012, and then renamed itself on May 16, 2013. WSCUC

 9              characterizes itself as an institutional accrediting agency recognized by the U.S.
10
                Department of Education that serves public and private higher education institutions
11
                around the world. WSCUC alleges that its accreditation aids institutions in developing
12
                and sustaining effective educational programs and assures the educational community and
13
                the general public that an accredited institution has met high standards of quality and
14

15              effectiveness. However, WSCUC has not met its obligations as a California Nonprofit

16              Corporation. WSCUC did not file its Statement of Information, which was due on
17              December 31, 2022. The failure to file can result in a monetary penalty and the suspension
18
                or forfeiture of its California registration. If WSCUC’s registration is lost or suspended, it
19
                cannot operate legally in California, including losing its ability to defend itself in Court. In
20
                August 2025, WSCUC attempted to file a California Form RRF-1with the California
21
                Department of Justice but was rejected because it had never filed the Initial Registration
22

23              Form (Form CT-1). WSCUC’s failure to comply with California’s nonprofit corporate

24              requirements makes it more difficult for Plaintiff ITU to proceed with its civil complaint.
25        3. Plaintiff is unaware of the true names and capacities, whether individual, corporate,
26
                associate or otherwise, of the Defendants sued herein as Unknown Persons 1 through100
27
                or any of them, and for that reason sues said Defendants, and each of them, by such
28

                                                        2
     4907-7867-5263.12
           Case 5:25-cv-08277            Document 1        Filed 09/29/25       Page 3 of 12



 1              fictitious names. Plaintiff believes that various officers and directors of WSCUC, past and
 2              present, may have been involved in damaging Plaintiff. Plaintiff will seek leave of Court
 3
                to amend this complaint to state the true names and capacities of Unknown Persons 1
 4
                through 100, inclusive, when those names and capacities have been ascertained. Plaintiff
 5
                is informed and believes, and thereon alleges, that each of the Defendants designated
 6

 7              herein as an Unknown Persons is responsible for all, or a portion of, the harm suffered by

 8              Plaintiff, as alleged herein.

 9                                        JURISDICTION AND VENUE
10
          4. Jurisdiction is vested in the United States District Courts through 20 U.S.C. § 1099b
11
                regarding the improper termination of accreditation claim due to a violation of common
12
                law due process and through 28 U.S.C. § 1331 (federal question jurisdiction) regarding
13
                the claim under 42 U.S.C. § 1981 regarding termination of the accreditation contract
14

15              based upon the corporation’s ethnic characteristics.

16        5. The United States District Court can exercise Supplemental Jurisdiction over the
17              California state law claims of Breach of Contract, Breach of the Covenant of Good Faith
18
                and Fair Dealing, and Defamation pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1367 as they form part of the
19
                same case or controversy and arise from a common nucleus of operative fact.
20
          6. Venue is properly based in United States District Court for the Northern District of
21

22              California under 28 U.S.C. 1391 as both Plaintiff ITU and Defendant WSCUC are based

23              in that district.

24        7.    20 U.S.C. § 1099b(e) requires the submission of any dispute involving the termination of
25              accreditation to initial arbitration prior to any other legal action.
26
          8. WSCUC was formerly associated with the Council for Higher Education Accreditation
27
                (“CHEA”), which had an arbitration protocol in place.
28

                                                         3
     4907-7867-5263.12
           Case 5:25-cv-08277           Document 1       Filed 09/29/25      Page 4 of 12



 1        9. On or about December 17, 2024, without seeking the approval or agreement of ITU,
 2              WSCUC withdrew from its affiliation with CHEA.
 3
          10. WSCUC did not want to comply with CHEA’s standards involving DEI (Diversity,
 4
                Equity and Inclusion), which are important to ITU as a global and multiethnic institution
 5
                of higher education.
 6

 7        11. When WSCUC withdrew from its association with CHEA, WSCUC did not have an

 8              arbitration protocol in place through which ITU could demand arbitration after the

 9              withdrawal of its accreditation by WSCUC.
10
          12. ITU and WSCUC could not agree upon an arbitration protocol and therefore ITU is filing
11
                its complaint in accordance with 20 U.S.C. § 1099b(f) which states that any “civil action
12
                brought by an institution of higher education”…”involving the denial, withdrawal, or
13
                termination of accreditation of the institution of higher education, shall be brought in the
14

15              appropriate United States district court.”

16        13. ITU brings this action against WSCUC based largely upon WSCUC’s withdrawal of
17              ITU’s accreditation on June 27, 2025, and WSCUC’s discriminatory practices leading to
18
                the withdrawal of accreditation.
19
                                              GENERAL BACKGROUND
20

21        14. Accreditation of institutions of higher education in the United States is a voluntary

22              independent peer review process through which the quality of a college or university’s

23              programs, faculty, infrastructure, finances and student resources is evaluated.

24        15. Institutions of higher education have the right to choose whether or not to participate in

25              the accreditation process, which is a voluntary, self-regulatory system.

26        16. The U.S. Department of Education does not accredit colleges and universities in the

27              United States.

28

                                                        4
     4907-7867-5263.12
           Case 5:25-cv-08277           Document 1         Filed 09/29/25     Page 5 of 12



 1        17. Instead, the Council for Higher Education Accreditation (“CHEA”) and the U.S.
 2              Department of Education provide oversight of the nongovernmental accrediting agencies
 3              that conduct the accreditation process.
 4        18. While accreditation is not a mandatory requirement for a college or university to operate
 5              in the United States, accreditation is necessary as a practical matter for an institution of
 6              higher education to admit certain categories of students.
 7        19. Students from foreign countries who want to study in the United States have to navigate
 8              through various governmental channels to obtain the Visas necessary for entry into the
 9              United States.
10        20. The Student and Exchange Visitor Program (SEVP) is part of U.S. Immigration and
11              Customs Enforcement (ICE) that oversees the Student and Exchange Visitor System
12              (SEVIS), which monitors nonimmigrant students (F-1, M-1 visas) and their dependents.
13        21. SEVP’s role in student immigration involves certifying schools to enroll foreign nationals,
14              tracking students’ records, and ensuring compliance with U.S. immigration laws.
15        22. SEVP certifies academic and vocational institutions to host nonimmigrant students.
16        23. An SEVP certified school issues a Form I-20 (“Certificate of Eligibility for Nonimmigrant
17              Student Status”) to a prospective student. The prospective student then uses the Form I-20
18              to apply for a student visa through the U.S. Department of State, which also oversees the
19              process.
20        24. While it is not mandatory for either the Student and Exchange Visitor Program (SEVP) as
21              part of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) or the United States
22              Department of State to require that an institution of higher education which is located in
23              the United States to be accredited before foreign students can enroll, as a practical matter,
24              both ICE and the US Department of State defer to college accreditors investigation of
25              colleges and universities rather than conducting their own independent investigations.
26                       FACTUAL ALLEGATIONS SPECIFIC TO THE COMPLAINT
27        25. ITU is a nonprofit global institution of higher education founded in 1994 and based in
28              Santa Clara, California.

                                                          5
     4907-7867-5263.12
           Case 5:25-cv-08277            Document 1        Filed 09/29/25      Page 6 of 12



 1        26. Institutions of higher education in the United States have the right to pursue their own
 2              educational mission and values, which is a right inherent in institutional autonomy.
 3        27. ITU emphasizes the STEM fields (Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics) in
 4              its course offerings.
 5        28. ITU provides its course offerings to students from around the world with the majority of
 6              its students coming from India and the People’s Republic of China.
 7        29. Both SEVP and the U.S. Department of State rely heavily upon the accreditation status of
 8              an institution of higher education in making the decision about whether or not to issue a
 9              visa to a prospective nonimmigrant student.
10        30. Institutions of higher education have the right to select an accreditor
11        31. ITU entered into an accreditation agreement with Defendant WSCUC in 2012.
12        32. In July 2018, WSCUC reaffirmed ITU’s accreditation for a period of six years.
13        33. In choosing Defendant WSCUC as its accreditor, ITU relied upon WSCUC’s statements
14              that it does not discriminate on the basis of race, color, religion, national or ethnic origin,
15              sex gender identity, sexual orientation or disability in its accreditation activities.
16        34. ITU expected WSCUC to act in a nonbiased manner during the ongoing accreditation
17              evaluation process.
18        35. When ITU chose WSCUC to act as its accreditor, WSCUC was affiliated with CHEA as
19              an overseer of WSCUC’s accreditation practices.
20        36. CHEA was committed to the inclusion of Diversity, Equity and Inclusion (“DEI”) in its
21              accreditation evaluation oversight.
22        37. Given the nature of ITU’s international student body, DEI is important to the ongoing
23              STEM programs being offered at ITU.
24        38. In December 2024, without consulting with or obtaining the permission of ITU, WSCUC
25              withdrew from its affiliation with and oversight by CHEA largely because of CHEA’s
26              inclusion of DEI in the accreditation evaluation process.
27        39. ITU was willing to and did provide WSCUC with all information necessary to evaluate
28              the quality of ITU’s program.

                                                         6
     4907-7867-5263.12
           Case 5:25-cv-08277              Document 1     Filed 09/29/25        Page 7 of 12



 1        40. In response, WSCUC stonewalled ITU and did not allow it to provide the information
 2              necessary to properly and reasonably evaluate ITU as a multiethnic institution of higher
 3              education.
 4        41. WSCUC’s act of withdrawing ITU’s accreditation on June 27, 2025 was based upon bias
 5              and fear rather than any reasonable evaluation of the facts.
 6        42. WSCUC is worried about losing its own certification by the U.S. Department of
 7              Education as a nongovernmental accrediting agency rather than acting as a proper
 8              accreditor.
 9
                                       FIRST CAUSE OF ACTION:
10                             VIOLATION OF COMMON LAW DUE PROCESS
11        43. Standards for the due process which Defendant as an accrediting agency must provide to
12              member institutions of higher education are established by Congress and the United States
13              Department of Education. (20 U.S.C. § 1099b; 34 (C.F.R. §§ 602.20, 602.25)
14        44. When an accreditor wishes to enforce its standards against a member and withdraw
15              accreditation, the accrediting agency has a duty to provide due process throughout. The
16              accreditor must, inter alia:
17                   a. “Provide the institution or program with a written timeline for coming into
18                       compliance that is reasonable . . . [and up to] four years” (34 C.F.R. §
19                       602.20(a)(2));
20                   b. “Follow its written policies and procedures for granting a good cause extension
21                       that may exceed the standard [four year] timeframe described in paragraph (a)(2)
22                       of this section when such an extension is determined by the agency to be
23                       warranted” (34 C.F.R. § 602.20(a)(3));
24                   c. Apply clear standards and apply such standards with consistency (34 C.F.R. §
25                       602.18(a)-(b));
26                   d. Use “procedures that afford an institution or program a reasonable period of time
27                       to comply with the agency’s requests for information and documents” (34 C.F.R. §
28                       602.25(b)); and

                                                         7
     4907-7867-5263.12
           Case 5:25-cv-08277             Document 1        Filed 09/29/25         Page 8 of 12



 1                   e. Provide institutions the right to appeal any adverse action prior to the action
 2                       becoming final including “the right to . . . employ counsel to represent the
 3                       institution or program during its appeal, including to make any presentation that
 4                       the agency permits the institution or program to make on its own during the
 5                       appeal.” (34 C.F.R. § 602.25(f)(2)).
 6        45. Defendant failed to comply with these requirements.
 7        46. Under its 2013 Handbook of Accreditation Defendant promised to:
 8                   a. “Apply with good faith effort its procedures and standards as fairly and
 9                       consistently as possible.” (WSCUC 2013 Handbook of Accreditation, at 5.);
10                   b. “Provide institutions a reasonable period of time to comply with Commission
11                       requests for information and documents.” (Id.);
12                   c. “Value the wide diversity of institutions it accredits and consider an institution’s
13                       purpose and character when applying the Standards.” (Id.); and
14                   d. [W]hen an institution failed to meet one or more of the Standards, “notify the
15                       institution of these findings and give the institution up to two years from the date
16                       of this action to correct the situation.” (Id. at 44.)
17        47. Defendant failed to meet its own promised standards.
18        48. WSCUC did not have appropriate evidentiary standards in place for the submission of
19              sworn statements or certified documents to support a member institution’s argument for
20              continued accreditation.
21        49. In withdrawing ITU’s accreditation without providing a reasonable amount of time for
22              ITU to submit supporting evidences, denying ITU requests for reasonable extensions of
23              time and a good cause continuance, WSCUC failed to follow its own policies and
24              practices and applicable federal law, and acted unreasonably, arbitrarily, and capriciously.
25              ITU was denied due process as a result.
26        50. Throughout the process of accreditation review, WSCUC did not acknowledge or
27              meaningfully respond to ITU’s objections and communications outlining procedural
28              concerns and due process failures.

                                                          8
     4907-7867-5263.12
           Case 5:25-cv-08277           Document 1        Filed 09/29/25       Page 9 of 12



 1     51.      A decision by an accrediting association is invalid if the decision is arbitrary capricious, or
 2              unreasonable.
 3        52. Plaintiff was harmed because of WSCUC’s failure to satisfy due process.
 4        53. Plaintiff suffered and continues to suffer financial losses, reduced student enrollment, and
 5              reputational harm, among other harms, because of WSCUC’s arbitrary and capricious
 6              decision to withdraw ITU’s accreditation.
 7
                                         SECOND CAUSE OF ACTION:
 8                                         BREACH OF CONTRACT
 9        54. Plaintiff ITU entered into an accreditation contract with Defendant WSCUC in 2012.
10        55. In July 2018, WSCUC reaffirmed ITU’s accreditation for a period of six years.
11        56. The accreditation contract included oral, written, and implied-in-fact terms.
12        57. The terms of the accreditation contract were clear enough that both parties could
13              understand what each was required to do.
14        58. The terms of the contract included that Plaintiff would pay Defendant required fees and
15              that in return Defendant would provide Plaintiff accreditation services.
16        59. Plaintiff did all, or substantially all, of the significant things that the contract required it to
17              do, including providing Defendant with access to all information required to conduct a
18              reasonable accreditation evaluation.
19        60. Despite Plaintiff continuing to fulfill all of its obligations under the accreditation contract,
20              on June 27, 2025, Defendant withdrew its accreditation of Plaintiff.
21        61. Plaintiff has been harmed as a result of Defendant’s action.
22        62. Defendant’s breach of contract was a substantial factor in causing Plaintiff’s harm.
23
                                 THIRD CAUSE OF ACTION:
24               BREACH OF THE COVENANT OF GOOD FAITH AND FAIR DEALING

25        63. Plaintiff ITU and Defendant WSCUC entered into an accreditation contract in 2012.

26        64. The accreditation contract entered into between Plaintiff and Defendant included an

27              implied promise of good faith and fair dealing.

28

                                                        9
     4907-7867-5263.12
          Case 5:25-cv-08277           Document 1        Filed 09/29/25       Page 10 of 12



 1        65. Plaintiff did all, or substantially all, of the significant things that the contract required it to
 2              do, including providing Defendant with access to all information required.
 3        66. All conditions required for Defendant’s performance of its obligation to accredit Plaintiff
 4              occurred.
 5        67. Rather than meet its obligations under the accreditation contract, on June 27, 2025,
 6              Defendant withdrew its accreditation of Plaintiff.
 7        68. By doing so, Defendant did not act fairly and in good faith.
 8        69. Plaintiff was harmed by Defendant’s conduct and its entitled to monetary damages,
 9              including punitive damages, according to proof.
10                                       FOURTH CAUSE OF ACTION:
11                                         DEFAMATION PER SE
          70. Defendant made statements that Plaintiff was unfit to operate an institution of higher
12
                education, and was withdrawing its accreditation of Plaintiff as a result.
13
          71. Defendant’s statements were false and were presented as facts, not just an opinion.
14
          72. Defendant communicated its statements to the U.S. Department of State, the U.S.
15
                Department of Homeland Security, and published the statements on its website which is
16
                accessible by the public.
17
          73. Defendant was at least negligent in determining the truth or falsity of its statements.
18
          74. Plaintiff has been damaged as a result of Defendant’s statements, and is entitled to
19
                monetary damages, including punitive damages, according to proof.
20

21                                   FIFTH CAUSE OF ACTION:
                            RACIAL DISCRIMINATION IN THE MAKING AND
22                          ENFORCEMENT OF CONTRACTS (42 U.S.C. § 1981)
23        75. Plaintiff ITU was founded by an individual of Chinese descent and has a multiethnic
24              identity. Plaintiff stands by the principle of protecting its students from the People’s
25              Republic of China, India, and other foreign countries, from racial discrimination
26        76. Plaintiff was a party to an accreditation contract with Defendant.
27        77. Plaintiff attempted but was unable to enjoy all benefits, privileges, terms and conditions of
28              the contractual relationship.

                                                       10
     4907-7867-5263.12
          Case 5:25-cv-08277             Document 1        Filed 09/29/25     Page 11 of 12



 1        78. Plaintiff’s inability to enjoy all benefits, privileges, terms and conditions of the contractual
 2              relationship was because of Defendant’s purposeful discrimination against the Plaintiff on
 3              the basis of Plaintiff’s race.
 4        79. Plaintiff has been damaged by Defendant’s purposeful discrimination, and is entitled to
 5              monetary damages, including punitive damages, according to proof.
 6
                                        FIFTH CAUSE OF ACTION:
 7                             FOR INJUNCTIVE AND DECLARATORY RELIEF
 8                                        (28 U.S.C. § 2201 et seq.)
       80.      Justiciable and actual controversies exist before this Court with respect to Defendant’s
 9
                breach of its accreditation contract with Plaintiff and improper withdrawal of Plaintiff’s
10
                accreditation.
11
       81. A declaratory judgment resolving this question is likely to prevent future harm to Plaintiff
12
                resulting from ongoing disputes between Plaintiff and Defendant and clarify or settle the
13
                legal rights of the parties to this action.
14
       82.      Plaintiff will suffer irreparable injury if Defendant’s withdrawal of Plaintiff’s
15
                accreditation is permitted to stand. If equitable relief is not granted, international students
16
                may be unable to attend ITU because such students will be denied access to necessary F-1
17
                visas, which must be certified by the Student and Exchange Visitor Program (“SEVP”).
18
       83.      Plaintiff has been damaged as a result of Defendant’s actions.
19
                WHEREFORE, Plaintiff ITU respectfully requests:
20
                     a) Monetary damages, including punitive damages, according to proof;
21
                     b) A declaration that WSCUC improperly withdrew ITU’s accreditation, and that
22
                         WSCUC’s determination is therefore vacated;
23
                     c) A permanent injunction vacating WSCUC’s decision withdrawing ITU’s
24
                         accreditation, and returning the parties to the positions they were in prior to
25
                         WSCUC’s withdrawal of ITU’s accreditation;
26
                     d) An Order retaining jurisdiction over this matter to enforce the terms of the foregoing
27
                         injunctive relief;
28

                                                         11
     4907-7867-5263.12
          Case 5:25-cv-08277             Document 1        Filed 09/29/25     Page 12 of 12



 1                   e) Such other and further relief as this Court may deem just and proper.
 2

 3                                            JURY TRIAL DEMAND
 4              Plaintiff demands a jury trial in this matter.
 5
